statement: An open tube, a cylinder with no top or bottom, is 5 cm tall and has a circumference of 12 cm. An ant on the outside walks from a point on the bottom rim to the point on the top rim exactly halfway around the tube. How long is the shortest such walk, in cm?

choices.misconception: I walked up the side and then straight across the top, as if the tube had a lid, but there is no top to walk across.
I walked straight up 5 cm and then 6 cm around the rim, instead of going diagonally.
I unrolled the tube but used the full circumference, 12, instead of the halfway distance of 6.

choices.text: the square root of (25 + 36 pi squared)
choices.misconception: I treated 12 cm as the diameter, so I thought half the circumference was 6 pi.

hints: Cut the tube along a straight line and flatten it.

Unrolling turns the curved surface into a rectangle without changing distances along it. The shortest walk on the surface becomes a straight segment on the rectangle; find its horizontal and vertical parts.
On the flattened rectangle the two points are 6 cm apart horizontally and 5 cm apart vertically.

solutions.reliable: Slit the tube along a vertical line away from the path and unroll it into a 12 cm by 5 cm rectangle. The start and end points are half the circumference, 6 cm, apart horizontally and 5 cm apart vertically. The shortest walk is the straight segment between them, of length the square root of (6 squared + 5 squared) = the square root of 61, about 7.8 cm. The transferable idea: to find a shortest path on a surface that can be flattened, flatten it and draw a straight line.
solutions.elegant: Going round the other way is the same length by symmetry, so either unrolling gives the answer, and no walk can beat a straight line on the flat sheet.

whyOnTest: Unrolling a cylinder turns a curved shortest path into a hypotenuse, and every distractor is a path you get by not unrolling, or by unrolling carelessly.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
